asDecan.p: Astrologers split each sign into three ten-degree slices, called decans, and give each one a planet. Your Sun sits between ten and nineteen degrees of Libra, the middle slice, where the sign is at full strength, and the Golden Dawn hands that stretch to Saturn. Saturn is exalted in Libra. That's the old word for a planet being an honoured guest, so this is about as good as Saturn gets. Venus still rules the sign, which is why you care whether everyone is getting on, but Saturn adds weight and a long memory. The Two of Swords just before you belongs to the Moon and sits blindfolded, putting a decision off. The Four after you belongs to Jupiter and is lying down, resting. Yours is the one that actually looks at what happened. Justice is still your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it. And yes, it's the card with the heart and the three swords, which people tend to find alarming the first time they see it.

When a friend rings to say they've been dumped, you're the one who asks what actually happened, in order, and then listens to the whole thing without jumping in. You're good at hard phone calls generally. At work you're the person who says in the meeting that the project isn't going to make the deadline, after everyone else has been nodding along for a fortnight. At a family dinner you notice who didn't get asked about their week, and it bothers you all evening. You keep old cards and letters, even from people you no longer speak to, because throwing them out feels like pretending it didn't happen. And you tend to know quite early when a friendship is running down. You can feel it weeks before anyone says so, usually from something small, like the replies getting shorter.

The less obvious gift is how you end things. Most people either drag a relationship out for a year too long or leave with a slammed door. With Saturn here you can close a chapter cleanly and still be decent about it. You'll have the proper conversation, give the books back, and say the kind thing at the end without lying. I've seen people with the Sun in this part of Libra stay on good terms with an ex for twenty years, and it isn't because the breakup didn't hurt. It's because they didn't need to turn the other person into a villain to get through it. The same shows up at work. When a team gets restructured and somebody has to tell six people their jobs are gone, you can do it in a way that means they still shake your hand afterwards.

The quieter trouble is that you grieve things before they've happened. A new relationship is going well and part of you is already working out how it ends, and whose fault it'll be. There's a ledger too. Libra wants things even and Saturn keeps records, and between them you can carry a list of every time you gave more and got less, going back years. You'd never say it at the time. It comes out eighteen months later, in one calm, complete sentence during an argument about the dishwasher, and the other person has no idea where it came from. And you can stay too long. If you promised, you keep turning up to the friendship or the committee well after it stopped working, because leaving would feel like breaking your word, and that's a bit of a problem.

Bad news makes you go very still. The first thing you do is get the facts straight, who said what, what it means for the rent, and you can look eerily calm doing it. People around you sometimes take this for not caring. A week later the feeling turns up, often all at once and somewhere inconvenient, like the supermarket car park. The risk after that is that you go grey for a while. You keep working and you answer messages, but everything's a bit flat, you stop suggesting plans, and your partner or your flatmate ends up tiptoeing around you without knowing why. What helps is plain structure for the body. Proper meals, a walk every day even in bad weather, bed at a set time, and one plan a week with a friend that you don't cancel.

You take love seriously, which sounds obvious for a Libra, but with Saturn in the mix it means you want to know where it's heading fairly early, and you mean the promises if you make them. Libra's opposite sign is Aries, and a lot of people with this Sun end up with someone quicker and hotter-tempered, someone who says the thing straight away while you're still weighing it. That can be good for you. The less obvious thing is that you need to be allowed to be sad inside a relationship without it being treated as a fault to fix. A partner who panics every time you go quiet, or tries to cheer you up in the first five minutes, wears you out. You do best with someone who'll sit on the couch with you and let a bad day just be a bad day.

Saturn exalted likes rules that are fair and applied the same way to everyone, so you suit work where that matters. Mediation, HR done properly, family law, compliance, editing, auditing, a union role, palliative care, running a support group, or being the one on the board who actually reads the whole report. You're good at delivering bad news, and organisations quietly lean on that. The catch is that you become everyone's messenger. The manager who can't face telling the client sends you, and the colleague who wants to complain about a teammate asks you to raise it. Over a few years that wears on you, especially when it's unpaid and unthanked. Ask for the title and the money that go with the responsibility, and let someone else carry the next one.

At twenty this slice of Libra usually feels old for its age. There's often an early loss or a first big heartbreak that hits harder than friends expect, and a habit of taking relationships very seriously while everyone else is being casual about them. You can seem a bit grave at parties, to be honest. By the mid-thirties Saturn tends to start paying off, as it does in most charts. You've been through a few real endings, you know you come out the other side, and you're less frightened of the next one, so you get warmer and a lot funnier. The fifties often bring people to your door. A friend going through a divorce, a colleague whose mother has died, a niece with her first broken heart. They come because you've been there and you don't flinch.

The next time something hurts, a remark at work, a friend cancelling again, tell one person about it within a day, before you've made up your mind about who was in the wrong. Say it messily. 'That stung and I don't know why yet' is enough. You're used to presenting your feelings once they're sorted and fair, and this gets them out while they're still just feelings. Do it three times over the next few months and notice how differently people respond to you.
